1: In exile by the river Chebar, the priest Ezekiel sees a storm cloud, four living creatures with four faces, wheels within wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with a figure like a man.
God's glory is not tied to Jerusalem; it comes to the exiles.
2: A voice tells Ezekiel to stand and sends him to Israel. He is to speak whether they listen or not. A scroll full of lament is held out to him.
The prophet's task is faithfulness, not success.
3: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it is sweet as honey. God makes him a watchman: if he fails to warn the wicked, he will answer for their blood.
Those who know the truth are responsible for passing it on.
4: Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on a brick, lays siege to it, lies on his side for many days and eats rationed bread.
A message acted out for people who have stopped listening.
5: Ezekiel shaves his head and burns, strikes and scatters the hair in thirds.
A picture of what will happen to Jerusalem's people.
6: The hilltop shrines will be destroyed. A remnant in exile will remember God.
"They shall know that I am the Lord," the book's refrain.
7: Disaster is at the door. Silver and gold will be thrown in the streets, unable to save.
Wealth is useless on the day of judgement.
8: In a vision Ezekiel is carried to Jerusalem and shown idols and pagan rites inside the Temple itself.
The worst idolatry is inside God's own house.
9: A man with a writing case marks the foreheads of those who grieve over the city's sins. The rest are struck down.
The mark, the letter tau, has been seen as a figure of the cross.
10: Burning coals are scattered over the city. The glory of the Lord rises from the Temple to its threshold.
God is leaving the house his people have defiled.
11: Corrupt leaders are judged. To the exiles God promises, "I will remove the heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh." The glory leaves the city.
God himself will be a sanctuary for the scattered.
12: Ezekiel digs through a wall and carries out his baggage in the dark as a sign.
The people say the vision is for far-off days; God says it is now.
13: False prophets cry "Peace" and paint over a cracked wall. It will fall.
14: Elders come to consult Ezekiel with idols set up in their hearts. Even Noah, Daniel and Job could save only themselves.
No one can lean on another's holiness.
15: Vine wood is good for nothing but burning. So is unfaithful Jerusalem.
A vine exists to bear fruit.
16: God found Jerusalem as an abandoned baby, raised her, married her and adorned her. She used his gifts for prostitution. Yet he will remember his covenant.
A shocking picture of ingratitude and of mercy greater still.
17: A riddle about the king of Judah breaking his oath to Babylon and turning to Egypt.
God will plant a tender shoot that becomes a great cedar.
18: The people blame their parents' sins. God answers: the soul that sins shall die; a wicked person who turns will live.
"I have no pleasure in the death of anyone. Turn, and live."
19: Judah is a lioness whose cubs were captured, and a vine torn up.
A funeral song for the royal house.
20: God reviews Israel's story from Egypt on: rebellion at every stage, and God sparing them for his name's sake.
He will bring them into the bond of the covenant.
21: God's sword is sharpened and drawn against Jerusalem. The king's crown is removed "until he comes whose right it is".
A hint of the Messiah in the middle of judgement.
22: Jerusalem's sins are listed: bloodshed, contempt for parents, oppression of the stranger. God looked for someone to stand in the breach and found none.
Christ becomes the one who stands in the gap.
23: Samaria and Jerusalem are pictured as two sisters who chased foreign lovers.
Alliances with idolatrous powers end in ruin.
24: The siege begins. Ezekiel's wife, the delight of his eyes, dies, and he is told not to mourn, as a sign.
The prophet's own loss mirrors the loss of the Temple.
25: Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia are judged for gloating over Judah's fall.
God sees how we react to others' misfortune.
26: Tyre rejoiced at Jerusalem's ruin and will be scraped bare like a rock.
Profit from another's disaster is condemned.
27: Tyre is a splendid merchant ship, loaded with the world's goods, that sinks in the heart of the sea.
28: The ruler who said "I am a god" will die like a man. He was in Eden, perfect, until pride was found in him.
Tradition has read this as an image of Satan's fall.
29: Pharaoh, the great dragon of the Nile, will be hooked and thrown into the desert. Egypt was a staff of reed to Israel.
Do not lean on what cannot hold you.
30: The day of the Lord comes for Egypt and its allies. Pharaoh's arm is broken.
Human power is in God's hand.
31: Assyria was a towering cedar, cut down for its pride. Pharaoh will be the same.
32: Pharaoh goes down to the pit to join the fallen armies of other nations.
Every empire ends in the same grave.
33: Ezekiel is again appointed watchman. A fugitive arrives: the city has fallen. The people enjoy hearing Ezekiel but do not act.
Hearing sermons like love songs changes nothing.
34: Israel's shepherds fed themselves, not the flock. "I myself will search for my sheep. I will seek the lost and bind up the injured."
Jesus claims this role in John 10.
35: Edom nursed an ancient hatred and wanted Israel's land.
Old grudges bring their own ruin.
36: Clean water and a new heart
"I will sprinkle clean water on you. I will give you a new heart and put my Spirit within you."
The Church reads this of baptism and the gift of the Spirit.
37: Ezekiel prophesies over a valley of bones. They come together, take flesh, and breath enters them. Two sticks become one: Israel and Judah reunited under one shepherd.
God can raise what is dead. Read at the Easter Vigil.
38: In the latter days Gog of Magog leads a horde against peaceful Israel. God himself fights him.
The final assault of evil fails.
39: Gog's army falls; its weapons burn for seven years. God will no longer hide his face.
Revelation uses Gog and Magog for the last rebellion.
40: The vision of the new Temple
Fourteen years after the fall, a man with a measuring rod shows Ezekiel a new Temple: gates and courts.
Hope is given a precise shape.
41: The inner rooms, the Holy of Holies and the carved decoration are measured.
42: Chambers where priests eat the holy offerings and change garments.
The holy is kept distinct from the common.
43: The glory of God comes from the east and fills the Temple. "This is the place of my throne."
The departure in chapter 10 is reversed.
44: The east gate stays shut because the Lord has entered by it. Rules are given for priests.
The Fathers saw in the closed gate a figure of Mary's perpetual virginity.
45: Land is set apart for the sanctuary and the prince. Use just balances.
46: Rules for Sabbath worship and the prince's offerings.
47: Water trickles from the threshold and becomes a river too deep to cross, making the Dead Sea fresh. Trees on its banks bear fruit every month.
A figure of grace flowing from Christ. Revelation ends with the same river.
48: The land is divided among the twelve tribes. The city's name will be "The Lord is there".
The goal of everything: God with his people.
